lines.text: Unit of a derived quantity, or is this equation possible? → build fundamental units from defining equations ($F = ma$, $W = Fs$, $Q = It$); every term must match, but a match can't show a missing $\frac{1}{2}$ or $2\pi$ ({{lesson:6.1}})
Estimate or order of magnitude → round to the nearest power of ten on a log scale: $a \times 10^{n}$ becomes $10^{n+1}$ when $a$ is above about $3.16$ ({{lesson:6.1}})

Forces or velocities at an angle → resolve each into perpendicular components ($\cos$ for the side next to the angle, $\sin$ for the side opposite), add each direction with signs, then combine with Pythagoras ({{lesson:6.2}})

Change in velocity when the direction changes → $\Delta\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{v}_\text{f} + (-\boldsymbol{v}_\text{i})$: reverse the initial velocity and add head to tail; along a line, give each velocity its sign first ({{lesson:6.2}})

Uncertainty in a calculated result → sums and differences: add absolute uncertainties; products and quotients: add fractional ones; a power $n$: multiply the fractional uncertainty by $\lvert n \rvert$ ({{lesson:6.3}})
Does a result agree with the accepted value? → see whether the accepted value lies inside value $\pm$ absolute uncertainty; if not, name a likely systematic error ({{lesson:6.3}})
Comparing two values → percentage error against an accepted value, percentage change from an original value, percentage difference (over the mean) when neither is the reference ({{lesson:6.3}})
Uncertainty in a gradient or intercept → draw the steepest and shallowest straight lines through every uncertainty bar; $\Delta(\text{gradient}) = \frac{\text{max} - \text{min}}{2}$ ({{lesson:6.4}})

Do the data support $y \propto x$? → draw the best line without forcing it through the origin, then check whether some straight line through the origin passes through every uncertainty bar ({{lesson:6.4}})

Testing a predicted relationship → rearrange it into $y = mx + c$ and plot those quantities ($T^{2}$ against $m$, $I$ against $\frac{1}{d^{2}}$); for $y = kx^{n}$ with $n$ unknown, plot $\log_{10} y$ against $\log_{10} x$ and the gradient is $n$ ({{lesson:6.4}})
